data.name: InnerCube
data.detailed_description:
Think, Roll, Match, Survive!

InnerCube is an action-puzzle game, where you control a multi-colored cube using the keyboard to navigate around a grid. Capture colored tiles by rolling the identical color on the cube on top of a tile.
Choose from two different modes: a challenging Puzzle Mode where every move counts or a fast and frantic Survival Mode!
  • How long can you survive?
  • 100+ Puzzle Levels and 7 Sectors.
  • Unlock new levels, Gold Status and Perfect Status in Puzzle Mode.

Puzzle Mode

  • Solve Puzzle levels by collecting color tiles.
  • 105 levels of mind bending action.
  • Earn Gold status by completing a level under the target number of moves; earn Perfect status by completing a level in the minimum number of moves possible.

Survival Mode

  • Score as many points as you can before getting trapped!
  • Collect bombs to get yourself out of trouble.
  • Capture tiles in quick succession for huge combo bonuses!
  • 30 different score rankings.

reviews.review:
InnerCube is a focused puzzle game that turns the simple act of rolling a colored cube into a demanding exercise in spatial awareness and route planning. Developed and published by Schell Games, it avoids unnecessary complexity and instead builds nearly the entire experience around understanding how each movement changes the cube’s orientation. The objective may initially appear straightforward: move across a grid and collect colored tiles by matching them with the correct face of the cube. In practice, however, every roll affects which color faces downward, so reaching a tile is only useful when the cube arrives in the correct orientation. This deceptively simple rule gives InnerCube much of its challenge and personality.

The Puzzle Mode forms the main attraction, offering 105 stages divided among seven sectors. Each level asks players to determine an effective sequence of movements while keeping track of both position and rotation. A direct route across the board is not necessarily the correct route because approaching a colored tile from the wrong direction can leave an incompatible face underneath the cube. As puzzles become more complicated, players must visualize several moves ahead and consider how every turn influences subsequent possibilities. The controls remain accessible throughout, allowing the difficulty to come from reasoning rather than mechanical execution.

Completing a puzzle is only the first level of accomplishment. InnerCube encourages efficient solutions through Gold and Perfect objectives. Gold rewards players for finishing within a specified number of moves, while Perfect demands the theoretical minimum. This gives completed stages meaningful replay value because an improvised solution can later be refined into something considerably more elegant. Searching for unnecessary movements and discovering shorter routes becomes almost a puzzle within the puzzle. Players interested only in progression can still move forward, while completionists have much tougher goals to pursue.

Survival Mode provides a useful change of pace by applying the same basic mechanics under greater pressure. Instead of methodically searching for an optimal solution to a predetermined stage, players attempt to accumulate points while avoiding situations in which further movement becomes impossible. Quickly collecting tiles produces combo bonuses, encouraging decisive play rather than prolonged contemplation. Bombs can also be collected and used to escape difficult situations. With 30 score rankings to work through, Survival Mode gives score-focused players a reason to repeatedly test their ability to recognize useful moves quickly.

The two modes complement each other particularly well. Puzzle Mode encourages patience and careful analysis, while Survival Mode emphasizes adaptation and speed. The fundamental rules remain consistent, meaning skills developed in one mode remain valuable in the other. Familiarity with how the cube rotates gradually reduces the need to consciously calculate every movement, creating a satisfying sense of mastery. This is where InnerCube becomes more engaging than its modest appearance might initially suggest: progress comes not from acquiring powerful abilities but from becoming better at understanding the system.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and colorful geometric style that fits its mechanical priorities. The boards and colored elements are designed to communicate information clearly rather than provide elaborate scenery. That simplicity works in the game's favor because players need to identify colors, positions, and movement possibilities without unnecessary visual interference. It has the character of a traditional abstract puzzle game, placing readable design and functional presentation above cinematic spectacle.

Its narrow focus can nevertheless be a disadvantage depending on what a player expects. InnerCube does not rely on storytelling, exploration, character development, or extensive mechanical variety. Most of its longevity comes from increasingly complicated variations of cube rotation and color matching. Anyone who does not find the core concept appealing may encounter repetition relatively quickly. Puzzle enthusiasts, on the other hand, may appreciate this consistency because the game spends its time exploring the consequences of a well-defined rule instead of constantly introducing unrelated mechanics.

The inclusion of achievements, rankings, minimum-move challenges, and Survival Mode gives the package additional replayability beyond simply finishing every stage once. Particularly dedicated players can pursue Perfect solutions across the puzzle collection, while score chasers can concentrate on improving Survival performances. This creates different standards of success without making the basic game inaccessible. A newcomer can understand what needs to be done almost immediately, yet achieving consistently optimal solutions requires substantially more thought.

InnerCube ultimately demonstrates how a small mechanical idea can support a surprisingly substantial puzzle game when developed carefully. Schell Games succeeds in transforming movement itself into the central problem: every step simultaneously changes location and orientation, forcing players to consider two interconnected variables. The 105 Puzzle Mode stages provide the structured challenge, while Survival Mode introduces a faster and more reactive interpretation of the same concept. Its minimalist nature means it will appeal most strongly to players who enjoy logic, optimization, spatial reasoning, and score chasing rather than those seeking narrative or extensive variety.

Its presentation and overall scope are modest, but the central cube-rolling mechanic has enough depth to support clever puzzles and rewarding optimization. The combination of accessible rules, increasingly demanding spatial challenges, Perfect-solution hunting, and a contrasting Survival Mode makes it a thoughtfully designed puzzle experience that gets considerable mileage from a remarkably simple premise.

Rating: 7/10
